question: What does the Bible say about whether God chooses who will be saved?
intro: Christians read the Bible as saying that God chooses people and appoints them beforehand, and they ask whom God chooses, on what basis, and to what end. The New Testament speaks of the elect, of election and of being predestined, and the Hebrew Scriptures speak of God choosing a people. This page sets the main readings side by side, each in the words its holders use, and chooses none of them. How a person's own will answers God's is treated on a separate card, free will.

agreed.summary: Every reading below takes the text to say that God chooses, that the choosing is made in Christ and for holiness, that it rests on God's grace and on no merit of the people chosen, and that those called the elect are to live as God's own people. The readings differ on whom the choosing includes, on what it rests, and on how it stands beside the call that goes out to everyone.

passages.quote: For He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless in His presence.
God chose you from the beginning to be saved by the sanctification of the Spirit and by faith in the truth.
passages.note: Some ancient manuscripts read “as firstfruits” in place of “from the beginning”.

passages.quote: as the elect of God, holy and beloved, clothe yourselves with hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience.

readings.label: God's choosing in view of faith: God foreknows who will trust in Christ and chooses them (what is called conditional election)
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to say that God wants everyone to be saved, and that God chooses for glory those whom he foreknows will trust in Christ, so that the choosing answers faith and does not come before it. They read the “foreknew” of Romans 8:29 and the “foreknowledge” of 1 Peter 1:2 as naming what the choosing rests on. John Wesley's sermon On Predestination states this reading, with God's foreknowing causing nothing that he foresees, and many Wesleyan and Methodist members hold it; the Methodist Articles of Religion have no article on predestination, and Wesley's sermon Free Grace rejects the teaching that God appoints any person to condemnation before the world began. Holders of this reading add that God's grace goes before every human response and makes trust possible for everyone (what is called prevenient grace), so that faith is a gift received and no one's own achievement. Eastern Orthodox readers speak of God's will that all be saved and of a lifelong cooperation with grace. The Confession of Dositheus (1672) speaks of God's predestining in view of how each would use the freedom God gave, with grace offered to all, and rejects election that rests on God's will alone; the Longer Catechism of Philaret teaches predestination as God's will to give all people the means to happiness, and cites the foreknowing of Romans 8:29. The Assemblies of God states this reading in its position paper on the assurance of salvation, and many other Pentecostal and Charismatic members hold it. Anabaptist confessions do not use the language of election or foreknowledge; the Mennonite confession of 1995 says God offers salvation to all and that a person's acceptance is a voluntary decision. Many Lutherans in the older dogmatic tradition state election as made in view of faith; the Brief Statement of the Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod rejects that phrase. Many Anglican, Baptist and free-church members hold this reading, and members of those traditions differ among themselves. The Catholic Church has not ruled between its schools on whether God's choosing rests on a foreseen response or on God's purpose alone, some Catholic theologians state it this way, and the Catechism (600) says God's plan of predestination includes each person's free response to his grace.

passages.quote: For those God foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers.
passages.note: Read as placing God's knowing beforehand ahead of his predestining.

passages.quote: according to the foreknowledge of God the Father and sanctified by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling by His blood
passages.note: Read as naming foreknowledge as the measure of the choosing named in 1 Peter 1:1.

passages.quote: who wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
passages.note: God's desire reaches everyone.

passages.quote: not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance.
passages.note: God's patience is for everyone to come to repentance.

passages.quote: For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life.
passages.note: The gift is for the world, and believing is the way it is received.

passages.quote: “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”
passages.note: Salvation promised to everyone who calls.

passages.quote: how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling!
passages.note: Read as a longing that the people's own unwillingness left unmet.
passages.context_note: The verse opens with whom he is speaking to: 'O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her'. The 'you' and 'your children' are Jerusalem's.

passages.quote: Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked? declares the Lord GOD. Wouldn't I prefer that he turn from his ways and live?
passages.note: Cited by holders of this reading: God's stated pleasure is in the turning and living of the wicked.

passages.quote: those He predestined, He also called; those He called, He also justified; those He justified, He also glorified
passages.note: The same people who were foreknown and predestined are called, justified and glorified.

passages.quote: God's set plan and foreknowledge
passages.note: Jesus was delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge, the two named together; holders of this reading take “foreknowledge” here as knowing beforehand.

passages.quote: He was known before the foundation of the world
passages.note: Christ was known before the foundation of the world and revealed in the last times.

passages.quote: In Him we were also chosen as God's own, having been predestined according to the plan of Him who works out everything by the counsel of His will,
passages.note: Believers are chosen and predestined in Christ, according to the plan of Him who works out everything by the counsel of His will.

passages.quote: the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, have obtained it, a righteousness that is by faith
passages.note: Gentiles who were not pursuing righteousness have obtained it by faith.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take Romans 9 to speak of God's freedom to choose peoples and persons for his purposes in history, as Jacob and Esau stand for two nations (Genesis 25:23, Malachi 1:2) and Pharaoh's hardening follows his own (Exodus 8:15), and not to fix each person's final end beforehand. They take the drawing of John 6:44 as reaching everyone, since Christ says he will “draw everyone” to himself (John 12:32), and they take “appointed for eternal life” in Acts 13:48 as describing those who had set themselves to receive the word. They take the choosing of Ephesians 1:4 as a choosing in Christ, so that those chosen are those who are in him by hearing and believing (Ephesians 1:13). Some holders take the choice of Jacob over Esau to rest on what God foreknew each of them would do, and grant that God's knowing carries love (Amos 3:2) while taking foreknowledge to be knowledge of the response.

readings.label: God's choice before the foundation of the world, resting on his own purpose and not on anything foreseen in the chosen (what is called unconditional election)
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to say that God chose those he saves before the world began, according to his own purpose, mercy and good pleasure, and not on account of anything foreseen in them, faith included, which God grants to those he chose. They read Israel's election as the pattern: God set his affection on a people for no merit of theirs. Reformed readers state this as the root of grace and of assurance. The Westminster Confession (chapter 3, held by the Presbyterian Church in America and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church) and the Canons of Dort (held by the Christian Reformed Church) also state that God passes over the rest and condemns them for their sin, which they call reprobation, and they deny that God is the author of sin; some call this double predestination and others avoid the term, and the Westminster Confession says the doctrine is to be handled with special prudence and care. Lutheran readers hold that God chose those he saves in Christ (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration XI), and decline to say that God chose any for condemnation; they differ among themselves on whether the choosing was made in view of faith. Catholic teaching in the Augustinian and Thomist line holds that God's predestination of the saved is wholly gracious, and denies that God predestines anyone to sin or to condemnation (Catechism 1037; Council of Trent, Session 6, canon 17); Trent warns against presuming to know that one is among the predestined (Session 6, chapter 12). The Church of England's Article XVII speaks of predestination to life in Christ, and says nothing of those passed over or of any foreseen faith; Anglicans have read it in the sense of this reading and in the sense of the first. The Second London (1689) Baptist Confession, chapter 3, states this reading, including God's leaving others in their sin; the Baptist Faith and Message (2000) of the Southern Baptist Convention names election as God's gracious purpose without saying whether it rests on foreseen faith, and Southern Baptists hold this reading and the first. Many Anglican and Baptist members hold this reading, and others in those traditions hold the first.

passages.quote: He predestined us for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of His will,
passages.note: The predestining is placed in the good pleasure of God's will.

passages.quote: The LORD did not set His affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous than the other peoples, for you were the fewest of all peoples.
passages.note: A choosing that rests on God's love and not on anything in the people chosen. Deuteronomy 7:6-8 is read whole by both readings.

passages.quote: Yet before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad, in order that God's plan of election might stand,
passages.note: The choosing is made before anything is done, so that it rests on God's plan.

passages.quote: So then, it does not depend on man's desire or effort, but on God's mercy.
passages.note: The outcome rests on God's mercy.

passages.quote: Therefore God has mercy on whom He wants to have mercy, and He hardens whom He wants to harden.
passages.note: Mercy and hardening both placed in God's will.

passages.quote: No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him, and I will raise him up at the last day.
passages.note: Coming to Christ is traced to the Father's drawing, which ends in being raised up.

passages.quote: and all who were appointed for eternal life believed.
passages.note: Believing follows the appointing.

passages.quote: not because of our works, but by His own purpose and by the grace He granted us in Christ Jesus before time began.
passages.note: Salvation and calling rest on God's purpose and grace given before time began.

passages.quote: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion
passages.note: God says to Moses that he will have mercy on whom he has mercy and compassion on whom he has compassion.

passages.quote: Does not the potter have the right to make from the same lump of clay one vessel for special occasions and another for common use?
passages.note: Paul's picture of the potter and the clay, in the middle of his argument about God's choosing.

passages.quote: Everyone the Father gives Me will come to Me
passages.note: Those the Father gives to Jesus will come to him.

passages.quote: no one can come to Me unless the Father has granted it to him
passages.note: Jesus says that coming to him is something the Father grants.

passages.quote: You did not choose Me, but I chose you
passages.note: Jesus tells his disciples that he chose them, and that they did not choose him.

passages.quote: those He predestined, He also called
passages.note: The ones God predestined are the ones he called, justified and glorified.

readings.answers: Many holders of this reading take “foreknew” in Romans 8:29 and “foreknowledge” in 1 Peter 1:2 to mean God knowing a person in love and setting his regard on them, as in “Only you have I known from all the families of the earth” (Amos 3:2), and not knowing beforehand what a person will do. They take 1 Timothy 2:4 and 2 Peter 3:9 to speak of people of every kind (see 1 Timothy 2:1-2) or of what God desires as distinct from what he purposes to bring about, and John 3:16 and Romans 10:13 to give the call that goes to everyone, with faith itself granted by God (Ephesians 2:8, Philippians 1:29). They take Matthew 23:37 to speak of the refusal of those who heard the call. Lutheran readers take 1 Timothy 2:4 and 2 Peter 3:9 of God's sincere will that every person be saved, and hold that those who perish do so by rejecting the Word (Formula of Concord, Epitome XI and Solid Declaration XI); they do not read these verses as limited to every kind of person.

readings.label: God's choosing of a people in Christ: Christ is the Chosen One, Israel and the church are chosen peoples, and individuals share in the choosing by being in him (what is called corporate election)
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to speak first of Christ as God's Chosen One, and then of a chosen people in him, so that the choosing is of a people and a person shares in it by being in Christ. They point out that the “us” and “you” of Ephesians 1 are plural, and that the Hebrew Scriptures speak of God choosing Israel as a people. Catholic teaching speaks of the Church as the new People of God, a chosen race (Lumen Gentium 9), and also of God's predestining of individuals (Catechism 600); the two are not set against each other. Anabaptist readers name the church as a chosen people (1 Peter 2:9); the Dordrecht Confession (1632) calls the church the chosen generation and names Christ as the one known before the foundation of the world (1 Peter 1:20). The Assemblies of God position paper on the assurance of salvation speaks of the predestination of the corporate body of Christ and sets it apart from predeterminism. Some Wesleyan and Methodist, Baptist and free-church members hold this reading, often together with the first, and members of those traditions differ among themselves. Some Reformed members, and Lutheran teaching, give weight to election in Christ as the place where election is found, beside the second reading. Christians who hold this reading differ on how the church's election stands beside Israel's, and Romans 11:28-29 is cited in that discussion.

passages.quote: The LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for His prized possession out of all peoples on the face of the earth.
passages.note: The choosing is of a people. Deuteronomy 7:6-8 is read whole by both readings.

passages.quote: Here is My Servant, whom I uphold, My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights.
passages.note: Holders of this reading follow Matthew 12:18 in taking this verse of Christ, the Chosen One. In Isaiah the servant is also called Israel (Isaiah 41:8, 49:3), and Jewish interpreters commonly read the servant of this passage as Israel.

passages.quote: This is My Son, whom I have chosen. Listen to Him!
passages.note: The Son is the one chosen.

passages.quote: It is not as though God's word has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel are Israel.
passages.note: Read as speaking of who belongs to the chosen people.

passages.quote: Regarding the gospel, they are enemies on your account; but regarding election, they are loved on account of the patriarchs.
passages.note: Election is named of a people, Israel, and Christians differ on what it says of Israel today.

passages.quote: And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise.
passages.note: Belonging to Christ places a person among Abraham's heirs.

passages.quote: you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession,
passages.note: The church is addressed as a chosen people.

passages.quote: And in Him, having heard and believed the word of truth-the gospel of your salvation-you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit,
passages.note: Read as saying how those chosen in him come to be in him.

passages.quote: the living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious in God's sight
passages.note: Christ is the living stone, chosen and precious in God's sight.

passages.quote: fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household
passages.note: Gentile believers are no longer strangers but fellow citizens with the saints.

passages.quote: you, a wild olive shoot, have been grafted in among the others
passages.note: Gentile believers are grafted into the olive tree, among the branches that remain.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take Romans 9 to speak of nations and of who counts as Israel in God's plan (Genesis 25:23, Romans 9:6), with the “children of the promise” of Romans 9:8 being those who share Abraham's faith (Galatians 3:29). They take the verses of drawing and appointing (John 6:44, Acts 13:48) as God gathering a people through the gospel, and the verses of foreknowledge and predestining (Romans 8:29-30) as God's plan for a people conformed to the image of his Son.

terms.note: The Berean's word for God's choosing in Romans 9:11, Romans 11:28 and 2 Peter 1:10; the related word “elect” renders the Greek for “chosen” (Colossians 3:12, 1 Peter 1:1).
The text's word in Romans 8:29-30, Ephesians 1:5 and Ephesians 1:11; the Berean renders the same Greek verb “decided beforehand” in Acts 4:28 and “destined” in 1 Corinthians 2:7.
The text's words in Romans 8:29 and 1 Peter 1:2. Traditions differ on whether they mean knowing what a person will do or knowing a person in love.

The Reformed term, used also by others who hold the second reading, for a choosing that rests on God's purpose and on nothing foreseen in the chosen. Lutheran confessions speak of election in Christ. This is a label from later theological discussion, not a word of the text.
The term used for the first reading, in which God's choosing answers the faith he foreknows. This is a label from later theological discussion, not a word of the text.
The term for the reading in which the choosing is of a people in Christ, and individuals share in it by being in him. This is a label from later theological discussion, not a word of the text.
The Wesleyan term for God's grace that goes before any human response and makes trust possible.

A term from Reformed discussion for the teaching that God appoints some to salvation and some to condemnation for their sin. Reformed readers differ on how to state it; Lutheran and Catholic teaching decline it, as does John Wesley's sermon Free Grace.

further_reading.title: Council of Trent, Session 6, Decree on Justification, chapter 12 and canons 15-17
further_reading.says: Chapter 12 warns that no one should presume to know that he is among the predestined, and canon 17 condemns saying that only the predestined receive justifying grace while all others are predestined by divine power to evil.

further_reading.title: Second Vatican Council, Lumen Gentium (Dogmatic Constitution on the Church), paragraph 9
further_reading.says: It teaches that God chose the race of Israel as his people, and that those reborn through faith in Christ are the new People of God, a chosen race, a royal priesthood and a holy nation.

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 600 (Jesus Died Crucified)
further_reading.says: It teaches that God's eternal plan of predestination includes each person's free response to his grace.

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1037 (Hell)
further_reading.says: It teaches that God predestines no one to go to hell, and that going there requires a deliberate and persistent turning away from God.

further_reading.title: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem, 1672), Decree 3
further_reading.says: It states that God predestined to glory and condemned according to his foreknowledge of how each would use free will, that preventing grace is offered to all, and it rejects the view that God predestines or condemns without regard to people's works.

further_reading.title: The Longer Catechism of Philaret of Moscow, questions 121-125
further_reading.says: It calls predestination God's will to bring man to eternal happiness, teaches that God has predestined all people to receive preparatory grace and sufficient means, and cites Romans 8:29 and the Eastern Patriarchs' statement on God's foreseeing how people use free will.

further_reading.title: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, Article XI (Election)
further_reading.says: It grounds election in God's gracious will in Christ before the world began, and not in anything in us such as foreseen works or merit, affirms that God does not wish any to perish, and places the cause of unbelief in the human will and not in God's decree.

further_reading.title: Formula of Concord, Epitome, Article XI (Election)
further_reading.says: It distinguishes God's foreknowledge of all people from his election of the children of God, rejects the teaching that God is unwilling that all be saved and has ordained some to condemnation so that they cannot be saved, and places the cause of ruin in those who reject the Word.

further_reading.title: A Brief Statement of the Doctrinal Position of the Missouri Synod (1932), Of the Election of Grace
further_reading.says: It holds that the faith the elect have in time is one of the blessings God gives them through his eternal election and not a condition that comes before it, and so rejects election in view of faith.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 3 (Of God's Eternal Decree)
further_reading.says: It teaches that God chose a definite number in Christ without any foreseen faith or works, passed over the rest and ordained them to wrath for their sin, and that the doctrine is to be handled with special prudence and care.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Shorter Catechism, questions 7 and 20
further_reading.says: Question 7 calls God's decrees his eternal purpose according to the counsel of his will, and question 20 says that out of his mere good pleasure he elected some to everlasting life from all eternity.

further_reading.title: Canons of Dort, First Main Point of Doctrine (Divine Election and Reprobation), articles 6, 7 and 15
further_reading.says: It teaches that God chose a definite number in Christ by sheer grace, rejects election on foreseen faith, and states that God passes over the rest and condemns them for their sins without being the author of sin.

further_reading.title: Belgic Confession, article 16 (The Doctrine of Election)
further_reading.says: It teaches that God rescues from the ruin of Adam's fall those he chose in Christ, from his eternal counsel and goodness without regard to their works, and is just in leaving the others in their ruin.

further_reading.title: Heidelberg Catechism, question 54 (the holy catholic church)
further_reading.says: It teaches that the Son of God gathers for himself, from the whole human race, a community chosen for eternal life, of which the believer is a living member.

further_reading.title: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 3, chapter 21 (Of the Eternal Election)
further_reading.says: Calvin teaches that by an unchangeable decree God freely chose some to salvation and left others to just condemnation, and that this shows salvation to come from God's mercy and not from human merit.

further_reading.title: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 3, chapter 22 (This Doctrine Confirmed by Proofs from Scripture)
further_reading.says: Calvin argues from Ephesians 1, Romans 9 and John that God's election rests on his own pleasure and not on foreseen merit, and answers objections to the doctrine.

further_reading.title: Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion, Article XVII (Of Predestination and Election)
further_reading.says: It calls predestination to life God's everlasting purpose to deliver those he chose in Christ out of mankind, says nothing of those passed over or of foreseen faith, and warns that the doctrine can lead curious and carnal persons to despair.

further_reading.title: John Wesley, Sermon 58 (On Predestination)
further_reading.says: Wesley teaches that God's foreknowledge causes nothing, that God foreknew believers as believers, and that the decree is that he who believes shall be saved.

further_reading.title: John Wesley, Sermon 128 (Free Grace), 1740
further_reading.says: Wesley rejects the teaching that God decrees some people to damnation, and holds that grace is free in all and for all, so that those who perish do so by refusing it.

further_reading.title: The Five Articles of the Remonstrants (1610), an Arminian text from before Wesley, Article 1
further_reading.says: Article 1 states conditional election: God, in Christ and before the foundation of the world, chose to save through those who believe in Jesus by the Spirit's grace and persevere, and leaves the unbelieving under wrath.

further_reading.title: James Arminius, A Declaration of the Sentiments (1608), on predestination, an Arminian text from before Wesley
further_reading.says: Arminius rejects the teaching that God absolutely elects some and reprobates others without regard to sin or righteousness, and holds that God's decree regards persons as believers.

further_reading.title: Second London (Baptist) Confession of 1689, chapter 3 (Of God's Decree), paragraphs 2-5
further_reading.says: It teaches that God chose a definite number in Christ without anything in the creature as a condition or cause, and left others to act in their sin to their just condemnation.

further_reading.title: Baptist Faith and Message 2000, Article V (God's Purpose of Grace)
further_reading.says: It calls election God's gracious purpose to regenerate, justify, sanctify and glorify sinners, consistent with human free agency, and does not say that it rests on foreseen faith.

further_reading.title: Assemblies of God position paper, The Assurance of Salvation (2017)
further_reading.says: The paper speaks of the predestination of the corporate body of Christ, whom God foreknew would respond to the Spirit's conviction, and sets it apart from predeterminism.

further_reading.title: Dordrecht Confession of Faith (1632), articles III, IV and VIII
further_reading.says: Article III says Christ was known before the foundation of the world (1 Peter 1:20), article IV that he shed his blood for all men, and article VIII calls the church the chosen generation.

further_reading.title: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995), Article 8 (Salvation), commentary
further_reading.says: It states that God offers salvation to all people, that accepting it is a personal and voluntary decision, and it does not speak of election or predestination.

_review_2026_10_25.why: Removes the mismatch between prose and list; the summary already says they hold it beside the second reading.

_review_2026_10_25.why: True of all three and the sentence is the same for each, so no reading is singled out.

_review_2026_10_25.fix: Add Ephesians 1:11 to reading 2 (or swap John 15:16 for Acts 13:48)
_review_2026_10_25.why: Every option takes a strong verse out of reading 2 (the 9-passage version breaks the cap of 8; the swap removes Acts 13:48, which readings 1 and 3 answer by name), so which verse goes is the editor's call. Doug, 2026-10-25, rulings sheet: as recommended.

_review_2026_10_25.fix: Add Romans 11:32 to reading 1 and Romans 11:5 to reading 3 for the arc of Romans 9-11 and Israel's present standing
_review_2026_10_25.why: Each addition needs a verse taken out of lists already balanced at 8, and it brings Israel's present standing onto the card, which changes what the readings cover; left for the editor. Doug, 2026-10-25, rulings sheet: as recommended.

_review_2026_10_25.fix: Deuteronomy 7:7 and 7:6 notes: add that Deuteronomy 7:6-8 is read whole by both readings
_review_2026_10_25.why: Both notes now say the verses are one argument, so neither reading shows half of it; nothing in the sentence favours either.

_review_2026_10_25.fix: Ruling A applied to every held_by: a tradition is listed only where its own canonical document states the reading. Reading 1 now lists Eastern Orthodox and Pentecostal / Charismatic; reading 2 Reformed, Lutheran, Anglican and Baptist / free church; reading 3 Catholic, Anabaptist and Pentecostal / Charismatic. Wesleyan / Methodist, Anabaptist, Baptist, Catholic and Anglican leave reading 1; Catholic leaves reading 2; Wesleyan, Baptist, Reformed and Lutheran leave reading 3. The members who hold each reading without the document are said in the summaries.

_why: QUOTES: every quote was read against http://localhost:8012/api/verse and ticked: Eph 1:4 (stops at 'presence.'; the server's 'In love' belongs to verse 5), Eph 1:5, Eph 1:13; 2 Thess 2:13 (clause from 'God chose you'); Col 3:12 (clause from 'as the elect'); Rom 8:29, 9:6, 9:11, 9:16, 9:18, 10:13 (server wraps it in curly quotes and I kept them), 11:28; 1 Pet 1:2, 2:9 (clause); 1 Tim 2:4 (clause); 2 Pet 3:9 (clause); John 3:16, 6:44; Matt 23:37 (clause); Ezek 18:23; Deut 7:6 (clause), 7:7; Isa 42:1 (first clause; server opens with a curly quote I dropped); Luke 9:35 (the voice's words); Acts 13:48 (clause); 2 Tim 1:9 (clause from 'not because'); Gal 3:29. Cited inside answers or terms and ticked: Gen 25:23, Mal 1:2, Exod 8:15, John 12:32, Amos 3:2 (server: 'Only you have I known'), Phil 1:29, Eph 2:8, 1 Tim 2:1-2, Rom 9:8, 2 Pet 1:10, Acts 4:28 ('had determined beforehand' in the site's gloss, 'decided beforehand' in the Berean line), 1 Cor 2:7 ('destined'). All ticked. TEXT NOTE: 2 Thess 2:13 has a textual variant in the manuscripts ('from the beginning' against 'as firstfruits'); the Berean follows 'from the beginning'. Both readings of the card use the verse, so I quote the Berean and leave the variant here for reviewers to decide whether it needs a marker on the page. ORDER: by when each reading was first stated at length, as I read the history. First: choosing in view of faith, the common reading of the Greek-speaking church of the early centuries, which is also the Eastern Orthodox and later Wesleyan form. Second: choosing grounded in God's purpose alone, stated in the West from the fifth century and carried into the Reformation churches. Third: corporate election, which has roots in the reading of Israel and Christ as the chosen ones, and was stated in its present form in the twentieth century. The order is by date of articulation and does not rank; note that the dating of the first and second is approximate, since the early church fathers wrote in several ways. THREE READINGS: the familiar split is conditional against unconditional, and I added the corporate reading so that readers who hold it (and who would not recognise themselves in either of the others) are not folded into an opponent. It often overlaps the first, and the summary says so. PASSAGES: 8 in each reading, same count. HELD_BY: assignments are approximate and the summaries say where a tradition holds a reading in part or its members differ: Catholic appears in the first and second because the church has not decided between its schools (the two views were argued at length in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries and the church left both open); Baptist / free church appears in all three because Baptists divide (Particular and General); Anglican in the second (its articles state predestination to life) with members differing; Lutheran in the second, with the summary naming their refusal of double predestination; Pentecostal in the first and third. Nothing names a person, scholar or leader. WORDS: I checked the intro, summaries, answers and notes for 'but', 'however', 'actually', 'clearly', 'only', 'merely'. 'But' and 'only' appear inside quotes from the verses (2 Pet 3:9, Matt 23:37, Rom 9:16, 11:28, 2 Tim 1:9, Amos 3:2), which are the verses' own words. 'And not' states a tradition's own contrast, as in the finished faith-and-works card. LEFT OUT: (a) Rom 9:13 ('Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated'), Rom 9:21-23 (the potter and the vessels), Exod 4:21 and Rom 9:17 (hardening of Pharaoh) and Eph 1:11: the first, second and third readings all have a view of them, and I cited Gen 25:23, Mal 1:2 and Exod 8:15 in the first reading's answer; Rom 9:18 stands in the second reading because it is the hardest verse for the first reading to answer and the second reading's holders cite it first. A reviewer may want one of these in the second reading's list in place of Acts 13:48. (b) John 6:37, John 10:26-29 and John 17:2, 6, 9 (those the Father gives to the Son), Rom 8:33, 1 Thess 1:4 and 2 Pet 1:10 ('make your calling and election sure'), which are central to the second reading's argument and to the question of assurance and falling away; the latter belongs to the card on whether salvation can be lost, which I left to its sibling. (c) Rom 11:5-7 (the remnant chosen by grace) and Rom 11:25-32: Israel's present standing is a live question among Christians, and the third reading cites 11:28 with a note saying so; a rabbi reviewing should say whether Israel's election needs its own place or sentence, and whether Deut 7:6-8 appearing in two readings (verse 6 in the third, verse 7 in the second) reads as fair to the Hebrew text. (d) Jer 1:5, Isa 49:1, Eph 3:11, 1 Cor 1:26-29 (God chose the weak and foolish) and Matt 22:14 ('many are called, few are chosen') and Matt 24:22-31 (the elect gathered): left out for count. Matt 22:14 and 1 Cor 1:26-29 merit a slot if a reviewer attentive to how the card reads to people without status or power thinks a verse about the chosen being the low and despised belongs in the second or third reading; I think 1 Cor 1:27-28 would fit either. (e) Free will, the bondage of the will, total depravity and the question of whether the saved can fall away: left to their own cards. (f) The doctrine of limited atonement and the question of the fate of the unevangelised and of infants: neither is a question about election as the text states it, and each divides these same traditions. RELATED IDS: card ids checked on the server (api/entity): grace, faith, salvation, mercy, adoption, covenant, inheritance, hardened, gospel, people. Not used because they are not found or the server's name for the id does not match the word: election, predestination, foreknowledge, chosen, elect, remnant (found but named 'their excess'), purpose (found but named 'deeds'), call (named 'summoned'). Theme ids checked against api/majorthemes: deliverance, covenant, children_of_god, church, mercy_restoration. READER PASSES: Catholic: the first reading's Catholic note states the church has not ruled between schools, and the second names the Augustinian and Thomist line; please confirm it reads fair. Eastern Orthodox: predestination is used by Orthodox writers of the 'God's will for all' reading, and the summary says so without claiming a formal teaching. Lutheran: the second reading says they decline to say any were chosen for condemnation and that members differ on 'in view of faith'; this is the point on which Lutheran readers differ most. Reformed: double predestination is named as a term and as a point on which Reformed members differ; a Reformed reviewer should say whether the wording fits. Wesleyan: prevenient grace named as their term. Baptist: both Particular and General streams are covered by being listed in more than one reading. Pentecostal: listed in the first and third. Secular scholar: the readings are dated by when they were articulated; two terms ('conditional election', 'corporate election') are modern labels and are described as such. Biblical-theology teacher: the third reading begins with Christ as the Chosen One (Isa 42:1, Luke 9:35), which a reviewer should confirm is a fair account of the passage and not a Christian reading imposed on Isaiah.
